Beverage prices ease as supply prospects improve

John Baffes

Kaltrina Temaj

November 19, 2026

This page in:

English

English

Improving coffee and cocoa supplies are helping ease beverage prices, though El Niño continues to pose risks to production and market stability. / Image: Shutterstock

This blog post is part of a special series based on the October 2026 Commodity Markets Outlook, a report published by the World Bank Group. This series features concise summaries of commodity-specific sections extracted from the report. Explore the full report here.
 
The World Bank Group’s beverage price index edged down in the first half of November, following a 20 percent increase in 2026Q3 (q/q). Cocoa and coffee prices declined amid improving supply conditions, while tea prices remained broadly stable. The index is projected to fall by 24 percent in 2026, largely reflecting recovering coffee and cocoa supplies, before rising marginally in 2027 as cocoa prices strengthen and then stabilizing in 2028.
Coffee prices ease as supply prospects improve. After rising by about 8 percent in 2026Q3 amid weather-related supply disruptions, coffee prices edged down in November as supply prospects improved. In October, Arabica averaged about $7/kg, 17 percent below its year-earlier level, while Robusta approached $4/kg. Despite weather concerns, global coffee output is expected to rise by 6 percent to a record 190 million bags in 2026–27, marking a fourth consecutive annual increase. Reflecting stronger supplies, Arabica prices are projected to decline by 13 percent in 2026, followed by smaller declines in 2027 and 2028. Robusta prices are projected to fall by 21 percent in 2026 before stabilizing in 2027–28. Weather-related risks remain substantial. The ongoing strong El Niño could disrupt production through drought and heat in Viet Nam and Central America, erratic rainfall and higher temperatures in Brazil and Colombia, and crop diseases triggered by heavy rains in Brazil.

 
Cocoa prices stabilize following a sharp increase. Cocoa prices were broadly stable in the first half of November, following a 46 percent increase in 2026Q3 (q/q) amid concerns that El Niño could disrupt supplies from Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana, the world’s leading cocoa producers. Higher production in both countries is estimated to have lifted global output by 7 percent in the 2025–26 crop season, which ended in September, raising the stocks-to-grinding ratio to 43 percent, above its long-term average of 41 percent. However, the market is expected to tighten in 2026–27 as adverse weather and lower pod counts weigh on West African crops. Following a projected 37 percent decline in 2026, prices are forecast to rise by 10 percent in 2027 and stabilize in 2028 as supply and demand move broadly into balance. Weather is the main risk as El Niño has historically reduced yields by bringing drier conditions to rainfed cocoa-growing areas in Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana.

 
Tea prices edge down amid weak demand and ample supplies. The three-auction average edged lower in November after remaining broadly unchanged in 2026Q3 (q/q). Kolkata prices fell sharply, following a seasonal pattern, amid weak export demand and strong production. Colombo prices also eased as subdued demand outweighed weather-related output declines. Mombasa prices were little changed and stood 8 percent above their year-earlier level as softer demand offset lower production in Uganda and Tanzania. Despite adverse weather in southern India and Sri Lanka, rising output in northern India, Bangladesh, and Kenya has kept the global market well supplied. Tea prices are forecast to rise by 4 percent in 2027 and 2 percent in 2028 as demand recovers, particularly in the Middle East. Prolonged Red Sea shipping disruptions pose a downside risk by raising costs and dampening demand in the Middle East and North Africa, a key market for East African tea. Conversely, El Niño poses an upside risk if it reduces tea output and quality in Bangladesh and parts of India.
